paragraphs: Modesty! Sacred child of sensibility and reason! True delicacy of mind! May I presume, without blame, to inquire into your nature, and to trace to its hidden source the gentle charm that softens every harsh feature of a character and makes lovely what would otherwise inspire only cold admiration? You who smooth the wrinkles of wisdom, and soften the tone of the loftier virtues until they all melt into humanity! You who spread the airy cloud around love, heightening every beauty it half conceals, and breathing out those shy sweetnesses that steal into the heart and charm the senses — shape for me the language of persuasive reason, until I rouse my sex from the bed of flowers on which they lie idly sleeping their lives away!

When discussing the association of our ideas, I pointed out two distinct ways in which it works; and in defining modesty, it seems to me just as proper to separate two things. One is the purity of mind that chastity produces. The other is a simplicity of character that leads us to judge ourselves fairly, as far from vanity as from presumption, though by no means at odds with a lofty sense of our own dignity. Taken in this second meaning, modesty is that sobriety of mind which teaches a man not to think more highly of himself than he ought to think. It should be kept distinct from humility, since humility is a kind of self-abasement. A modest man often conceives a great plan and clings to it tenaciously, aware of his own strength, until success confers a sanction on it that settles its character. Milton was not arrogant when he let slip a judgment of his own that later proved a prophecy; nor was General Washington when he accepted command of the American forces. Washington has always been described as a modest man; yet had he been merely humble, he would probably have shrunk back irresolute, afraid to entrust himself with the direction of an enterprise on which so much depended.

A modest man is steady, a humble man timid, and a vain one presumptuous: this is the judgment that observing many characters has led me to form. Jesus Christ was modest, Moses was humble, and Peter vain.

Having thus distinguished modesty from humility on the one side, I do not mean to confuse it with bashfulness on the other. Bashfulness is in fact so distinct from modesty that the most bashful girl, or the rawest country lout, often becomes the most impudent; for their bashfulness is merely the instinctive timidity of ignorance, and habit soon turns it into brazen self-assurance.*

(*Footnote. “Such is the country-maiden’s fright, When first a red-coat is in sight; Behind the door she hides her face, Next time at distance eyes the lace: She now can all his terrors stand, Nor from his squeeze withdraws her hand, She plays familiar in his arms, And every soldier hath his charms; From tent to tent she spreads her flame; For custom conquers fear and shame.”)

The shameless behaviour of the prostitutes who crowd the streets of London, stirring pity and disgust by turns, may serve to illustrate this remark. They trample on maidenly bashfulness with a kind of bravado and, glorying in their shame, become more boldly lewd than men ever appear to be, however depraved — men to whom this sexual quality has not been gratuitously assigned. But these poor ignorant wretches never had any modesty to lose when they gave themselves up to infamy; for modesty is a virtue, not a quality. No, they were only bashful, shamefaced innocents; and when they lost their innocence, their shamefacedness was roughly rubbed away. A virtue, had it been sacrificed to passion, would have left some traces in the mind, making us respect the grand ruin.

Purity of mind, or that genuine delicacy which is the only virtuous support of chastity, is closely related to that refinement of humanity which is never found except in cultivated minds. It is something nobler than innocence: it is the delicacy of reflection, not the coyness of ignorance. The reserve of reason, which, like habitual cleanliness, is seldom seen in any great degree unless the soul is active, can easily be told apart from rustic shyness or wanton skittishness; and far from being incompatible with knowledge, it is knowledge’s fairest fruit. What a gross idea of modesty the writer of the following remark had! “‘The lady who asked the question whether women may be instructed in the modern system of botany, consistently with female delicacy?’ was accused of ridiculous prudery: nevertheless, if she had proposed the question to me, I should certainly have answered — They cannot.” So the fair book of knowledge is to be shut with an everlasting seal! On reading similar passages I have reverently lifted up my eyes and heart to Him who lives for ever and ever, and said: O my Father, have You, by the very constitution of her nature, forbidden Your child to seek You in the fair forms of truth? And can her soul be sullied by the knowledge that solemnly calls her to You?

I have then pursued these reflections philosophically until I concluded that the women who have most developed their reason must have the most modesty — though a dignified composure of bearing may have replaced the playful, bewitching bashfulness of youth.*
(*Footnote. Modesty is the graceful, calm virtue of maturity; bashfulness, the charm of lively youth.)

This, then, is how I have argued. If chastity is to be the virtue from which unaffected modesty naturally flows, attention must be drawn away from occupations that exercise nothing but the sensibility, and the heart must be taught to beat in time with humanity instead of throbbing with love. A woman who has given a large share of her time to purely intellectual pursuits, and whose affections have been exercised by humane and useful plans, must, as a natural consequence, possess more purity of mind than those ignorant beings whose hours and thoughts are filled with gay pleasures or schemes for conquering hearts. Regulating outward behaviour is not modesty, though those who study the rules of decorum are, in general, called modest women. Make the heart clean; let it open out and feel for everything human, instead of being narrowed by selfish passions; let the mind often turn to subjects that exercise the understanding without inflaming the imagination — and unaffected modesty will put the finishing touches to the picture.

She who can make out the dawn of immortality in the streaks of light that shoot across the misty night of ignorance, promising a clearer day, will respect as a sacred temple the body that houses a soul capable of such improvement. True love, too, spreads this kind of mysterious sanctity around the beloved, making the lover most modest in her presence. Affection is so reserved that, in receiving or returning physical endearments, it wishes not only to avoid the human eye, as a kind of profanation, but to spread around itself a cloudy obscurity that shuts out even the impudent, sparkling sunbeams. Yet an affection does not deserve to be called chaste unless it takes on a sublime shade of tender melancholy, which lets the mind stand still for a moment and enjoy the present satisfaction, when a sense of the Divine presence is felt — for this must always be the food of joy!

As I have always liked to trace any prevailing custom back to its source in nature, I have often thought that the respect for relics, so much abused by selfish priests, was born of a feeling of affection for whatever had touched the person of an absent or lost friend. Devotion, or love, may be allowed to make the garments sacred as well as the person; for a lover must lack imagination who does not feel a sort of sacred respect for his mistress’s glove or slipper. He could not confuse them with ordinary things of the same kind.

This fine feeling, perhaps, would not bear analysis by the experimental philosopher — but of such stuff is human rapture made! A shadowy phantom glides before us, hiding every other object; yet when the soft cloud is grasped, the form melts into common air, leaving a lonely emptiness, or a sweet perfume stolen from the violet, which memory holds dear for a long time. But I have stumbled unawares onto fairy ground, feeling the mild breeze of spring stealing over me, though November frowns.

As a sex, women are more chaste than men; and since modesty is the effect of chastity, they may deserve to have this virtue attributed to them in a rather special sense. Yet I must be allowed to add a hesitant “if”: for I doubt whether chastity will produce modesty — though it may produce propriety of conduct — when it is merely a respect for the world’s opinion, and when flirtation and the lovesick tales of novelists occupy the thoughts. Indeed, experience and reason would lead me to expect more modesty among men than among women, simply because men exercise their understandings more than women do.

But as regards propriety of behaviour, women, with the exception of one class, clearly have the advantage. What can be more disgusting than that impudent dross of gallantry, thought so manly, which makes many men stare insultingly at every woman they meet? Is this respect for the sex? Such loose behaviour shows so much habitual depravity and such weakness of mind that it is useless to expect much public or private virtue until both men and women grow more modest — until men, curbing a sensual fondness for the sex, or an affectation of manly assurance (more properly, impudence), treat one another with respect, unless appetite or passion gives their behaviour its own particular tone. I mean even respect for the person — the modest respect of humanity and fellow-feeling; not the lustful mockery of gallantry, nor the insolent condescension of the protector.

To carry the observation further still, modesty must wholeheartedly disown, and refuse to live alongside, that debauchery of mind which leads a man coolly and without a blush to bring out indecent allusions or obscene witticisms in the presence of a fellow creature. Women are now out of the question, for in their presence it is brutality. Respect for man as man is the foundation of every noble sentiment. How much more modest is the libertine who obeys the call of appetite or fancy than the lewd joker who sets the table roaring with laughter!

This is one of the many cases in which the sexual distinction regarding modesty has proved fatal to virtue and happiness. It is, however, carried further still: woman, weak woman, made the slave of sensibility by her education, is required to resist that sensibility on the most trying occasions. “Can any thing,” says Knox, “be more absurd than keeping women in a state of ignorance, and yet so vehemently to insist on their resisting temptation?” Thus, when virtue or honour makes it proper to check a passion, the burden is thrown onto the weaker shoulders, contrary to reason and true modesty, which ought at least to make the self-denial mutual — to say nothing of the generosity of courage, supposed to be a manly virtue.

Rousseau’s and Dr. Gregory’s advice about modesty — strangely misnamed! — runs in the same vein; for they both want a wife to leave it in doubt whether sensibility or weakness led her into her husband’s arms. The woman who can let the shadow of such a doubt rest on her husband’s mind for a moment is immodest.

But let me put the subject in a different light. The lack of modesty, which I chiefly deplore as destructive of morality, arises from the state of warfare between the sexes that voluptuous men so strenuously uphold as the very essence of modesty, though it is in fact its bane. For this warfare is a refinement of sensual desire into which men fall who have not virtue enough to enjoy the innocent pleasures of love. A man of delicacy carries his notions of modesty further still, for neither weakness nor sensibility will satisfy him — he looks for affection.

Again: men boast of their triumphs over women. What do they boast of? Truly, that the creature of sensibility was surprised by her sensibility into folly — into vice;* and the dreadful reckoning falls heavily on her own weak head when reason wakes. For where are you to find comfort, forlorn and disconsolate one? He who ought to have guided your reason and supported your weakness has betrayed you! In a dream of passion you consented to wander through flowery meadows, and, heedlessly stepping over the precipice to which your guide lured you instead of guarding you from it, you start out of your dream only to face a sneering, frowning world, and to find yourself alone in a wilderness; for he who triumphed in your weakness is now pursuing new conquests. But for you — there is no redemption this side of the grave! And what resource do you have in an enfeebled mind to raise a sinking heart?
(*Footnote. The poor moth, fluttering round a candle, burns its wings.)
